ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Centro Superior de Estudios Universitarios La Salle (CSEULS-PI 010/2020).
All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were classified into two pre-existing clinical groups, while experimental conditions were assessed repeatedly within participants.
Participants were recruited through convenience sampling from specialized clinical settings and the university campus of the Centro Superior de Estudios Universitarios La Salle.
Based on their clinical characteristics and predefined eligibility criteria, participants were classified into two groups: a control group (CG; n = 42) and a neck pain group (NPG; n = 42).
Participants were asked to select the number that best represented their neck pain intensity during the preceding week.
Written informed consent was obtained before any study-related assessments were performed.
Participants were seated with their backs supported, feet resting on the floor, legs uncrossed and positioned approximately hip-width apart, and the cervical spine maintained in a neutral position.
Participants were seated with their backs supported, feet resting on the floor, and the cervical spine initially maintained in a neutral position.
Participants were instructed to perform active cervical movements while maintaining their trunk position to minimize compensatory movements.
A total of 84 participants were included in the study, comprising 42 healthy controls (CG) and 42 individuals with chronic neck pain (NPG).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample size estimation was performed using G*Power software (version 3.1.9.7; Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Germany). The calculation was based on a repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), considering the interaction between group (individuals with chronic neck pain and healthy controls) and experimental condition. Given the limited evidence regarding cervical muscle mechanical responses during tongue-pressure tasks, a medium effect size (f = 0.25) was assumed. The significance level was set at α = 0.05, with a statistical power of 80% (1 -β = 0.80). The final study sample comprised 84 participants, with 42 individuals in each group.

live_data_statements: Participants were classified into two pre-existing clinical groups, while experimental conditions were assessed repeatedly within participants.
Participants were recruited through convenience sampling from specialized clinical settings and the university campus of the Centro Superior de Estudios Universitarios La Salle.
Based on their clinical characteristics and predefined eligibility criteria, participants were classified into two groups: a control group (CG; n = 42) and a neck pain group (NPG; n = 42).
Participants were asked to select the number that best represented their neck pain intensity during the preceding week.
Written informed consent was obtained before any study-related assessments were performed.
Participants were seated with their backs supported, feet resting on the floor, legs uncrossed and positioned approximately hip-width apart, and the cervical spine maintained in a neutral position.
Participants were seated with their backs supported, feet resting on the floor, and the cervical spine initially maintained in a neutral position.
Participants were instructed to perform active cervical movements while maintaining their trunk position to minimize compensatory movements.
A total of 84 participants were included in the study, comprising 42 healthy controls (CG) and 42 individuals with chronic neck pain (NPG).
